title: A morning intention
tomorrow: why did Thoreau call a swim in a pond a religious exercise?

segments.voice: Yesterday, my morning line: Abba Isaac's one verse carried all day, and Benedict's monks reading on, page by page. A line says something. Today the morning aims at something.

Before a run, people set a pace on their watch. Islam has an older kind of aiming, and it begins with a journey. Sahih al-Bukhari opens its whole collection with Umar ibn al-Khattab on the pulpit, repeating what he heard the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, say. It was about the hijra, the migration to Medina, a road that cost people their homes. And the Prophet names someone who makes the very same journey for another reason: a woman he wants to marry. Does his journey count?
screen: `A PACE ON YOUR WATCH.` → `UMAR ON THE PULPIT.` → `THE SAME ROAD TO MEDINA.` → `DOES HIS JOURNEY COUNT?`

segments.voice: Here is the saying, in paraphrase. Actions are judged by intentions, and each person gets what they intended. Whoever migrated for God and His Messenger, their migration is for God and His Messenger. Whoever migrated for something of this world, or for a woman to marry, their migration is for what they migrated for. Same road. Same dust. Same new city. Two different journeys, and you can't tell them apart from the outside. Notice the man who traveled for love isn't cursed. He gets what he went for: a marriage. The point is the aim. That's the teaching, and it has a name: niyyah, intention. In Islamic teaching a prayer or a fast begins with niyyah, held in the heart; some say it in words too, others simply hold it. And by this hadith, even a meal or a day's work is weighed by the aim behind it. A hadith ties the fast to an intention made before dawn. So an ordinary act, aimed at something larger, becomes something larger. Something to tell a friend tonight: of all the sayings he gathered, Bukhari chose this one to put first. On your own path, borrowed with the tag on: this morning's acts may look a lot like yesterday's. The niyyah is what makes this day this day.
screen: `ACTIONS ARE JUDGED BY INTENTIONS.` · `SAME ROAD, TWO JOURNEYS.` · `NIYYAH, HELD IN THE HEART.` · `AN ORDINARY ACT, AIMED HIGHER.` · then, large: `TODAY I WILL.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand flat on your chest and feel it rise and fall for a few breaths. Then finish one sentence quietly, in your own words: today I will, and one aim, not a list. Keep the hand there while you mean it, the way niyyah is held in the heart.
A morning intention: the aim you set before the acts. In Islam, niyyah: the same road, a different journey.
Your line: today I will. One aim, set in the heart before the day's first act. Sixteen hundred days, done.

notes: 2026-10-15 v3: written new in recipe v3, shape senses. Story: Umar on the pulpit relating the hadith of intentions; the same hijra made for God and His Messenger or for a woman to marry (Bukhari 1). Teaching named: niyyah, intention held in the heart, by which Muslims understand prayer, fasting and ordinary acts to be weighed. The hand on the chest is this path's posture, offered as a way to feel 'held in the heart', not presented as a Muslim ritual.

Check: the paraphrase of Bukhari 1 (no translation quoted); 'a road that cost people their homes' as a description of the hijra; niyyah's place in the heart and 'some say it in words too' (schools differ on pronouncing it); the pre-dawn intention for the fast and the hadith numbers cited.
Check: the 'man who migrated for a woman' is named in the hadith text only as a type ('or a woman to marry'); the later commentators' story of Umm Qays's emigrant is left out.
